clinicalPearls: Metabolic syndrome is a clustering of metabolic abnormalities (central obesity, hypertriglyceridemia, low HDL cholesterol, hyperglycemia, and hypertension) that together raise the risk of cardiovascular disease and diabetes.

Diagnosis under NCEP:ATPIII (2001) requires three or more of: waist circumference >102 cm in men or >88 cm in women; triglycerides >=150 mg/dL; HDL <40 mg/dL (men) or <50 mg/dL (women); BP >=130/85 mmHg; fasting glucose >=100 mg/dL (or specific medication for, or prior diagnosis of, the relevant condition).

The Harmonizing definition uses ethnicity-specific waist circumference cutoffs (e.g., for South Asian and Chinese men >=90 cm, Europid men >=94 cm, Japanese men >=85 cm), reflecting that risk at a given waist circumference differs between populations.

Visceral (intra-abdominal) adipose tissue is more strongly linked to insulin resistance, diabetes, and CVD than subcutaneous fat, but waist circumference alone cannot reliably distinguish the two depots; DEXA, CT, or MRI is needed for that distinction.

Normal-weight individuals can still be insulin-resistant and meet criteria for metabolic syndrome, a phenotype that is particularly evident in populations from India, Southeast Asia, and Central America.
The syndrome is typically asymptomatic; physical examination often shows only elevated waist circumference and blood pressure, which should trigger a search for the other biochemical components.
Lipoatrophy and acanthosis nigricans, when present, signal severe insulin resistance, though they are far less common than the standard components.

Hypertriglyceridemia is an excellent marker of the insulin-resistant state; fasting triglycerides above roughly 180 mg/dL (~2.0 mM) are typically accompanied by a predominance of small, dense, more atherogenic LDL particles.
Most patients (~75%) with type 2 diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance have metabolic syndrome, and its presence in these groups marks a higher CVD burden than in those without the syndrome.

Conditions strongly associated with insulin resistance and the syndrome include metabolic-associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD/MASH), polycystic ovary syndrome, and obstructive sleep apnea, which should be screened for during evaluation.
Obstructive sleep apnea can predict metabolic syndrome even without excess adiposity, and insulin resistance tends to be more severe in apnea patients than in weight-matched controls.

Hyperuricemia reflects insulin-resistance-related defects in renal tubular handling of uric acid and may itself contribute to hypertension via effects on endothelial nitric oxide synthase and activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.
reference.pathophysiology: Insulin resistance is the most widely accepted unifying mechanism. Early insulin resistance manifests as postprandial then fasting hyperinsulinemia, eventually progressing to hyperglycemia as compensatory beta-cell secretion fails. An overabundance of circulating free fatty acids (FFAs), released from expanded adipose tissue and from lipoprotein-lipase-mediated lipolysis, drives the process: FFAs impair insulin-mediated glucose uptake in muscle, promote intramuscular and cardiac triglyceride accumulation, and increase hepatic glucose and triglyceride production with VLDL secretion. Insulin normally suppresses lipolysis (its most sensitive action), so resistance amplifies FFA release in a self-perpetuating loop. Increased VLDL/apoB and elevated apoC-III inhibit lipoprotein lipase, raising triglyceride-rich remnants; HDL becomes small, dense, and cleared faster, lowering HDL cholesterol. Loss of insulin-mediated vasodilation (nitric oxide) with preserved renal sodium reabsorption and sympathetic activation, plus adipose angiotensinogen expression, contributes to hypertension. Contributing/associated mechanisms include leptin resistance, reduced anti-inflammatory adiponectin, increased proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, IL-18, TNF-alpha, resistin) from adipose-derived macrophages, a prothrombotic state (fibrinogen, PAI-1), oxidative stress with mitochondrial dysfunction, and alterations in the gut microbiome (increased Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio).
additionalDifferentials: Type 2 diabetes mellitus / impaired glucose tolerance
Genetic lipodystrophies (e.g., Berardinelli-Seip congenital, Dunnigan familial partial lipodystrophy)
Cushing's syndrome / other endocrine causes of central obesity and hypertension
nonInfectiousMimics: Lipodystrophy syndromes (severe insulin resistance with many overlapping components)
Polycystic ovary syndrome with insulin resistance
additionalInvestigations: Fasting lipid panel (triglycerides, HDL cholesterol) and fasting glucose are required for diagnosis
Waist circumference measurement and blood pressure
Optional insulin-resistance biomarkers individualized to the patient: apoB, hsCRP, fibrinogen, uric acid, urinary albumin/creatinine ratio, liver function tests
Sleep study if symptoms of obstructive sleep apnea are present
If PCOS suspected (clinical features and anovulation): testosterone, luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone
MAFLD assessment via FIB-4 fibrosis score or elastography
DEXA, CT, or MRI if discrimination of visceral versus subcutaneous fat is needed
redFlags: Acanthosis nigricans or lipoatrophy indicating severe insulin resistance
Established type 2 diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance (markedly elevated diabetes and CVD risk)
Coexisting metabolic syndrome and elevated hsCRP (associated with increased all-cause mortality)
Features suggesting MASH/advanced liver fibrosis (precursor of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma)
reference.prognosis: Metabolic syndrome roughly doubles the risk of cardiovascular death and confers about a threefold higher risk of acute myocardial infarction or stroke; the risk for type 2 diabetes is increased three- to fivefold (fasting glucose explaining most of this). In the REGARDS cohort, metabolic syndrome carried a relative risk of about 1.34 for all-cause mortality, with the relationship to hsCRP and mortality stronger in white than in black participants. Prevalence among patients with coronary heart disease may reach up to 60% in those over 75. Risk and prevalence are modifiable: cardiac rehabilitation and lifestyle change (improved nutrition, physical activity, weight reduction) can reduce the prevalence of the syndrome.
pitfalls: Waist circumference does not reliably separate subcutaneous from visceral fat, so it can misestimate true metabolic risk without imaging.
A single ethnicity-blind waist cutoff under- or over-estimates risk across populations; ethnicity-specific thresholds are needed.
Normal body weight does not exclude the syndrome, so insulin resistance can be missed in lean individuals.
Whether metabolic syndrome adds CVD or diabetes risk beyond the simple sum of its individual components remains debated, so it should not be over-interpreted as an independent diagnosis.
Fasting insulin levels or HOMA capture only part of insulin resistance, so they inadequately quantify the contribution of resistance to hypertension.
Obstructive sleep apnea and PCOS are commonly overlooked associated conditions if not actively screened for.
reference.severityClassification: There is no graded severity scale; the syndrome is defined categorically by meeting three or more of the five diagnostic components (NCEP:ATPIII 2001 or the ethnicity-adjusted Harmonizing definition, Table 420-1). Risk rises with the number of components present and with associated markers such as elevated hsCRP.
management: Intensive lifestyle modification with a calorie-reduced diet, increased physical activity and weight loss is the first-line mainstay targeting the underlying insulin resistance
Treat atherogenic dyslipidaemia with a statin, adding a fibrate or other agent for persistent hypertriglyceridaemia
Control blood pressure, favouring renin-angiotensin system inhibitors given their metabolic profile
Address hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance with metformin alongside lifestyle measures to reduce progression to type 2 diabetes
Consider weight-loss pharmacotherapy such as a GLP-1 receptor agonist, or bariatric surgery, for obesity not controlled by lifestyle alone
Screen for and treat associated conditions — obstructive sleep apnoea and metabolic-dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease
Reduce global cardiovascular risk with smoking cessation and periodic monitoring of glycaemia, lipids and blood pressure

algorithms.title: Harmonized IDF/AHA/NHLBI Metabolic Syndrome Assessment and Cardiometabolic Risk Pathway

steps.action: Screen all patients with elevated BMI, central adiposity, or hypertension for the 5 standardized cardiometabolic criteria (waist circumference, triglycerides, HDL, blood pressure, fasting glucose).
Men: >= 102 cm (Caucasian) or >= 90 cm (South Asian, Asian, Hispanic). Women: >= 88 cm (Caucasian) or >= 80 cm (South Asian, Asian, Hispanic).
Triglycerides >= 150 mg/dL (1.7 mmol/L) AND/OR Reduced HDL-C (< 40 mg/dL in men, < 50 mg/dL in women) or specific drug treatment for dyslipidemia.
Systolic BP >= 130 mmHg or Diastolic BP >= 85 mmHg (or antihypertensive therapy) AND Fasting blood glucose >= 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) or drug treatment for elevated glucose.

Calculate 10-year ASCVD risk. Screen for Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatohepatitis (MASH / MASLD) using FIB-4 score. Comprehensive lifestyle intervention (Mediterranean diet, 150 min/wk moderate exercise) + statin for ASCVD risk + Metformin / SGLT2i / GLP-1 RA for cardiometabolic protection.
